html:
A Japanese carmaker founded in 1937 by Kiichiro Toyoda, now the largest maker of cars in the world. Its way of running factories, known as lean production, changed manufacturing everywhere.

The company grew out of a maker of automatic looms founded by Kiichiro's father, Sakichi Toyoda. It built trucks for the army during the war and was nearly bankrupt by 1950. Orders for trucks during the Korean War saved it.

In the postwar years the engineer Taiichi Ohno and others built the Toyota Production System. It made only what was needed, when it was needed ("just in time"), kept stocks low, and let any worker stop the line to fix a problem. It cut waste and raised quality without the vast stockpiles of the mass production pioneered by Henry Ford.

Small, reliable, fuel-saving Toyotas such as the Corolla sold well abroad, above all after the oil shocks of the 1970s. Toyota helped lead Japan's postwar boom alongside firms such as Sony, and in 1997 launched the Prius, the first mass-produced hybrid car.
